extracted.intended_audience: conference/journal peer reviewers and program chairs; early-career researchers learning to review
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for performing and managing high-quality peer reviews for conference papers (case-study: DocEng), including reviewer responsibilities, chair duties, review content and tone, and practical checks (plagiarism, reproducibility, statistics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Kindness
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame your review how you would like it framed if it were your paper being reviewed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This will ensure that the authors can use your review as a learning experience. Be kind, not sappy. Criticism is appropriate but should be delivered in a constructive tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasise the Good
rubrics_metrics.description: Highlight what you consider to be the single most influential idea the paper contains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use your position to identify and develop the core, differentiating contribution; helping authors focus on their paper's main impact is often more valuable than correcting small peripheral issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Background Research
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame the review within the context of existing research and verify that the paper is contributing new knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If not directly aligned with your projects, search the title/keywords on Google Scholar, find the top 1–3 papers in the area and check whether they are cited/discussed appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plagiarism and AI-Generated Content Checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Check that the paper has not been plagiarised or AI generated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search for rare terms on Google Scholar to see matches; use plagiarism detection software (Grammarly, Turnitin, etc.). Flag suspected fake reviews or paper-mill/AI issues to the chair.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether, assuming all resources were available, you would be able to repeat the experiment based on the paper's description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review with the intent to replicate: are procedures, data, parameter settings, and sufficient detail provided for replication?

rubrics_metrics.name: Materials and Methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the choice and completeness of materials and methods and suggest improvements or missing literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend alternative approaches or third‑party materials/methods if relevant. Avoid pushing your own citations, but note serious omissions and suggest concrete improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Are the Results Believable?
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the experimental data supports the claims made in the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check credibility: provide measures of variability, beware of n=1 experiments, and evaluate whether statistical tests (parametric/nonparametric, ANOVA, etc.) are used appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discussion Quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Check the discussion for appropriate interpretation of results and whether authors consider limitations or alternative explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for sensitivity analyses, checks for overfitting, and whether the experiments are tightly coupled to the claims. Suggest things authors may have tried or should try to strengthen discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjacencies / Applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess how close the work is to other potential applications and identify additional application areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors may not identify ideal applications; reviewers can add most value by pointing out adjacent application domains that broaden the paper's impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Longevity / Falsifiability (Will It Last?)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider factors that could deprecate or obviate the reported findings; check whether falsification scenarios are discussed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Popper’s Falsification Principle: authors should discuss scenarios where proposed theories fail. Results showing only supporting evidence raise suspicion of selective reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid One-Liners and Snark
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not submit terse, belittling, or snarky reviews (e.g., one-liners like 'Great paper; recommend acceptance.' or dismissive comments without constructive guidance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such reviews give no actionable feedback and can be disheartening. Even positive recommendations should explain why the paper is strong to help chairs and authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start Review with an Outline of Contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin your review with a few sentences describing the topic and basic contributions of the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This helps the program chair categorize the paper and signals to authors that you understood the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major Comments: Recommendation with Justifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide your recommendation and major comments explaining the reasoning behind it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use major comments to discuss clarity, soundness of approach, interpretation of results, and missing citations. These help chairs, other reviewers, and authors understand the decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minor Comments: Detailed Corrections and Suggestions
rubrics_metrics.description: Include additional comments for minor issues such as spelling, grammar, and suggestions for figures/tables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label these as minor so authors can prioritize major fixes first; be specific about small corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address Program Chair's Deciding Factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure your review explicitly addresses any points the program chair/editor has indicated should be deciding factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check the review form or instructions for required aspects and make sure you respond to them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review Revision and Clarity Check
rubrics_metrics.description: Re-read your review before submission to check for errors and clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take a step back and edit for tone and comprehensibility; the program chair may ask for rephrasing if language is inappropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocate Sufficient Time and Communicate Delays
rubrics_metrics.description: Allocate enough time to carry out an effective review within deadlines and inform the program chair if delays occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers should plan ahead; if a review will be late, always communicate with the chair so papers can be reassigned as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declare Conflicts of Interest and Maintain Integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Flag conflicts of interest so that you are not assigned papers by close collaborators; always act with academic integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid fake or favourable reciprocal reviews. If suspicious behaviour is detected, communicate it to the chair. Conflicts due to same institution or recent collaboration should be declared.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain Confidentiality and Avoid Using Unpublished Ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat submitted works in confidence and do not use authors' ideas for personal gain prior to publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a paper is accepted, cite it only after publication. If rejected, do not appropriate ideas; report concerns to the chair if misuse is suspected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer Load and Diversity (Chair Responsibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure reviewers are not overloaded and that the reviewer pool is diverse in expertise and experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DocEng aims for reviewers to handle ~2–3 full papers and ~2–3 short papers, with around a month to review. Balance experienced reviewers with newcomers for mentorship and diversity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer-Paper Matching and Bidding Process
rubrics_metrics.description: Use abstracts for bidding and match reviewers to papers based on expressed expertise; assign three reviewers per paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers rank interest/expertise after abstract submission; chairs pair three reviewers per paper, attempting to match expertise and keep assignments fair and unbiased.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent Reviews Followed by Controlled Discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain independent reviews initially (reviewers cannot see each other's reviews) and permit discussion after submission to resolve conflicts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independence helps prevent bias; once reviews are in, reviewers may see others' reviews and add further comments to address conflicts—these post-review comments are not shown to authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program Chair Moderation of Reviews and Tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Program chairs should read reviews to verify appropriate tone and constructiveness and may ask reviewers to revise or withdraw inappropriate reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chairs can rephrase reviews, request edits for tone, involve a fourth reviewer if needed, and regulate critique levels to reach a fair decision consistent with the conference program.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check for Paper-Mill and AI-Generated Submissions (Chair Duty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Before sending for review, chairs should cursory-review submissions to flag obvious irregularities like paper-mills or AI-generated papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This helps avoid wasting reviewer time and maintains the integrity of the review pool.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus Areas for DocEng Reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: At DocEng, reviewers are instructed to focus on novelty and originality, clarity and cohesiveness, and relevance to the DocEng community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These focal points give reviewers priorities and reduce unfounded or personal judgments. Tailor similar focal criteria to your conference's goals.
